scheme.node: A testable unit of knowledge. A node exists only if a definition or an exercise in the book targets it. Headers are narrative, not nodes.

kind.idea: A concept in the usual sense; ask Understand questions.
kind.result: An equation or fact derived from ideas; ask Remember or derive questions. Linked to the formula sheet by eq.
kind.skill: A procedure the book teaches and the exercises test on its own; ask Apply questions.

scheme.prereqs: Edges. Mastery propagates downward: mastering a node implies its prerequisites.
scheme.coverage: Which spans of the text introduce, use, or reinforce each node. Span ids are element ids, qualified by section: 2.5-notation.
scheme.ids: Canonical and book-independent, so another textbook's constant-acceleration section maps to the same nodes.
scheme.section: Section that introduces the node. Placeholders are nodes from sections not built yet; they resolve when that section is built.

concepts.name: Reference frame
concepts.why: A position is always given relative to something, such as the Earth, a whiteboard, or the cabin of an airplane. Choosing the reference frame is the first step in describing any motion.
concepts.evidence: Defined in the text ("position relative to a convenient reference frame"); the AP question separates position from displacement, which only makes sense once a frame is fixed.

concepts.name: Position
concepts.why: The position of an object is where it is at a particular time, given as a coordinate with a sign on the chosen axis. Every other quantity in one-dimensional kinematics is built from positions and times.
concepts.evidence: Glossary term; the AP question distinguishes position from distance traveled and displacement.

concepts.name: Displacement, $\kdx = \kxf - \kxo$
concepts.why: Displacement is the change in position, that is, the final position minus the initial position. It has a sign, and the sign gives the direction. In kinematics we nearly always deal with displacement rather than with the path taken.
concepts.evidence: Check Your Understanding (a); problems 1 and 3 part (c); AP question.

concepts.name: Distance (magnitude of displacement)
concepts.why: Distance is the magnitude of the displacement, so it has no sign. It is easy to confuse with distance traveled, which is why the text treats the two separately.
concepts.evidence: Check Your Understanding (c); problems 1 and 3 part (b); conceptual question 2.

concepts.name: Distance traveled (path length)
concepts.why: Distance traveled is the total length of the path, and it can be much greater than the magnitude of the displacement. For example, a professor who paces 150 m during a lecture may end up only 2.0 m from where she started.
concepts.evidence: Check Your Understanding (b); problems 1 and 3 part (a); conceptual questions 1 to 3.

concepts.name: Constant-acceleration model
concepts.why: In this section we assume that acceleration is constant. Then the average acceleration equals the acceleration at every instant, and the average velocity is simply the midpoint of the initial and final velocities. The kinematic equations all follow from this assumption, and many real motions can be described in pieces within which it holds.
concepts.evidence: Definition in the text ("acceleration is constant"); exercises ap-marble, p6, p18 test whether the learner knows when the model applies.

concepts.name: $\kx = \kxo + \kvb\kt$
concepts.why: Displacement equals the average velocity multiplied by the elapsed time. This is the definition of average velocity rearranged, so it holds whether or not the acceleration is constant.
concepts.evidence: Tested directly by p7, p8; used in p11, p13, p14.

concepts.name: $\kvb = \tfrac{\kvo + \kv}{2}$
concepts.why: When acceleration is constant, velocity changes at a steady rate, so the average velocity is the midpoint of the initial and final velocities. This step turns the definition of average velocity into the equations for displacement.
concepts.evidence: Tested by p7, p8; required to derive x-quadratic and v-squared.

concepts.name: $\kv = \kvo + \ka\kt$
concepts.why: The final velocity depends on both the size of the acceleration and the time over which it acts. A modest acceleration that lasts a long time can produce a very large velocity.
concepts.evidence: Tested by cyu-rocket, ai-rel-1, p1 to p5; used in most later problems.

concepts.name: $\kx = \kxo + \kvo\kt + \tfrac12\ka\kt^2$
concepts.why: Under constant acceleration, the displacement grows with the square of the elapsed time. For example, a dragster starting from rest covers only one quarter of the track in the first half of its run.
concepts.evidence: Tested by ai-rel-2, ap-marble, p5, p9, p10, p17.

concepts.name: $\kv^2 = \kvo^2 + 2\ka\kdx$
concepts.why: This equation relates velocity to displacement without involving time. Because the stopping distance of a car grows with the square of its speed, halving the speed reduces the stopping distance to one quarter.
concepts.evidence: Tested by ai-rel-3, p11 to p16, p18.

concepts.name: Choose the equation from knowns and unknowns
concepts.why: To solve a problem, first list the quantities you know and the quantity you want to find, and then choose the equation in which the quantity you want is the only unknown. This is the skill that Putting Equations Together teaches and that multi-step problems test.
concepts.evidence: Taught explicitly as a problem-solving strategy; tested by p5, p7, p19, p20, p21.

concepts.name: Interpret the solution physically
concepts.why: The algebra can give two roots, a negative time, or a square root with two signs, but only one of these describes the motion. Deciding which solution is physically reasonable is part of solving the problem.
concepts.evidence: Example 2.13 rejects the negative time root; p10(b) and p17 ask the learner to judge whether a result makes sense.
